chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's own order: fractals first, then solids. Each fractal is built one step at a time and its counts are predicted before they are revealed, so a picture becomes a rule (multiply by 8, multiply by 4). Solids are first pictured in the mind, then cut, unfolded, flattened onto a plane and finally drawn on an isometric grid.

points.title: Predict, then check
points.text: Each idea opens with a question answered before the reveal: how many squares at the next step, will this shape fold into a cube, is this path really the shortest.

points.title: Imagine before you handle
points.text: The book asks students to visualise first and only then use cutouts. The plan keeps that order: the video asks for a mental picture, and a tool appears only where handling the shape is the idea.

points.title: Tools only where manipulation is the concept
points.text: Ten tools, each used once: stepping three fractals, counting the parts of solids, folding and rolling nets, unfolding a box to find a path, tilting a solid to see its projection, turning a solid to read its views, and stacking cubes on an isometric grid. Topics about ideas carry no tool.

points.title: Many right answers
points.text: Profiles, projections and nets rarely have one answer. Students are asked for more than one solid that fits a view, and for every unfolding before choosing the shortest path.

modules.module_summary: Self-similar shapes in nature and in mathematics. The Sierpinski Carpet, the Sierpinski Triangle and the Koch Snowflake are built by repeating one rule; counting squares, holes, sides, area and perimeter step by step turns each picture into a pattern of numbers. Fractals in temples, blankets and prints close the module.

concepts.concept_name: A fern made of smaller ferns

content.text:
In this chapter, we will explore two geometric themes. We will study fractals which are self-similar shapes. They exhibit the same or similar pattern over and over again, but at smaller and smaller scales. We will then look at different ways of visualising solids.
4.1 Fractals
One of the most beautiful examples of a fractal that also occurs in nature is the fern. The fern is seen to have smaller copies of itself as its leaves, and these in turn have even smaller copies of themselves in their sub-leaves, and so on!
Similar phenomena of self-similarity occur in trees (where a trunk has limbs, and a limb has branches, and the branches have branchlets, and so on), clouds, coastlines, mountains, lightning, and many other objects in nature.
Other mathematical fractals can also be very beautiful. We will explore some of them here.

content.text:
1. Predict first: look at one leaf of a fern. Does it look like a small copy of the whole fern?
2. Each leaf is a smaller fern, and each sub-leaf is a smaller copy again. This is self-similarity.
3. Trees, clouds, coastlines and lightning repeat the same pattern at smaller scales. Can a rule in mathematics make a shape like this, one step at a time?

concepts.concept_name: Building the carpet step by step

content.text:
The Polish mathematician Sierpinski discovered a type of fractal known as the Sierpinski Carpet. It is made by taking a square, breaking it into 9 smaller squares, and then removing the central square; the same procedure is then repeated on the remaining 8 squares, and so on. One then sees the same pattern at smaller and smaller scales.
Draw the initial few steps (at least till Step 2) of the shape sequence that leads to the Sierpinski Carpet.
By its construction, each step in the sequence has (i) squares of the same size that remain in the figure, and the size of these squares becomes smaller and smaller as the step number increases, and (ii) square holes that are formed by removing square pieces.
Do you see any pattern in the number of holes and squares that remain at each step?

content.text:
1. Predict first: Step 1 leaves 8 squares. How many small squares remain after Step 2?
2. At Step 1 the square is split into a 3 by 3 grid and the centre is removed: 8 squares remain, 1 hole.
3. At Step 2 each of the 8 squares is split into 9 and loses its centre: 8 × 8 = 64 squares remain.
4. The 8 new centres are new holes, and the first hole is still there, so there are 1 + 8 = 9 holes.

content.text:
Worked example: Draw Steps 0, 1 and 2 of the Sierpinski Carpet and count the remaining squares and the holes at each step.
1. Step 0: one whole square, no hole.
2. Step 1: a 3 by 3 grid with the centre removed leaves 8 squares and 1 hole.
3. Step 2: each of the 8 squares loses its own centre, so 8 × 8 = 64 squares remain.
4. Holes at Step 2: the old hole plus 8 new ones, 1 + 8 = 9.
Answer: Remaining squares 1, 8, 64; holes 0, 1, 9

content.text:
Let Rn represent the number of remaining squares at the nth step, and Hn represent the number of holes at the nth step.
Every square that remains at a given step, say Step n, gives rise to 8 squares that remain at the (n + 1)th step. Thus, we have R(n + 1) = 8 Rn.
Can this be used to get a formula for Rn?
We have R0 = 1, R1 = 8 × 1 = 8, R2 = 8 × 8 = 8². In general, Rn is 8 to the power n.

2. Each remaining square becomes 8 remaining squares, so the count is multiplied by 8 at every step.
3. Starting from 1: 1, 8, 64, 512. The count at Step n is 8 multiplied by itself n times.

content.text:
Worked example: Find the number of remaining squares at Step 3 and at Step 4 of the Sierpinski Carpet.
1. Step 2 has 8 × 8 = 64 remaining squares.
2. Step 3: each of these gives 8, so 64 × 8 = 512.
3. Step 4: 512 × 8 = 4096.
Answer: 512 squares at Step 3 and 4096 at Step 4

concepts.concept_name: Holes: old holes plus one for every square

content.text:
Similarly, how do we find the number of holes at a given step?
Every square that remains at the nth step gives rise to a hole in the (n + 1)th step. All the holes present at the nth step remain in the (n + 1)th step as well. Thus, H(n + 1) = Hn + Rn.
So we have R0 = 1, H0 = 0; R1 = 8, H1 = 1; R2 = 8², H2 = 1 + 8; R3 = 8³, H3 = 1 + 8 + 8².

content.text:
1. Predict first: Step 2 has 9 holes. Is the number of holes at Step 3 equal to 64, or more?
2. The 64 squares of Step 2 each lose a centre at Step 3, making 64 new holes.
3. The 9 older holes remain, so Step 3 has 9 + 64 = 73 holes.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students draw Step 0, Step 1 and Step 2 of the Sierpinski Carpet and count the remaining squares and the holes at each step.
Students use the rule that each remaining square gives rise to 8 remaining squares at the next step to write Rn as 8 to the power n and find the count at Step 3 and Step 4.
Students use the rule that every remaining square makes one new hole while old holes stay to find the number of holes at any step.
Students step the Sierpinski Carpet forward, predict the remaining squares, holes and area left before each step, and check their predictions against the picture.

content.text:
Sierpinski came up with another fractal made in a similar way. An equilateral triangle is broken up into 4 identical equilateral triangles by joining the midpoints of the bigger triangle, and then the central triangle is removed. This procedure is repeated on the 3 remaining triangles, and so on.
Show that by joining the midpoints of an equilateral triangle, we divide it into 4 identical equilateral triangles. [Hint: Note that the corner triangles are isosceles.]
This fractal is called the Sierpinski Triangle/Gasket.

content.text:
1. Predict first: the triangle has side 8 cm. What is the side of each small triangle after joining the midpoints?
2. Each corner triangle has two sides of 4 cm (half of each side) with a 60° angle between them.
3. Two equal sides make the base angles equal; with 60° at the top, each base angle is (180° − 60°) ÷ 2 = 60°. So the corner triangle is equilateral with side 4 cm.
4. The middle triangle's three sides are the bases of the three corner triangles, all 4 cm, so it is equilateral too. All four are identical.

content.text:
Figure it Out (sierpinski fractals, question 1): Draw the initial few steps (at least till Step 2) of the shape sequence that leads to the Sierpinski Triangle.
1. Step 0: draw an equilateral triangle.
2. Step 1: join the midpoints of its sides and shade out the middle triangle; 3 triangles remain.
3. Step 2: repeat on each of the 3 corner triangles; 3 × 3 = 9 triangles remain.
Answer: Step 0 is one triangle, Step 1 shows 3 triangles around 1 hole, Step 2 shows 9 triangles and 4 holes

content.text:
Figure it Out (sierpinski fractals, question 2): Find the number of holes, and the triangles that remain at each step of the shape sequence that leads to the Sierpinski Triangle.
1. Each remaining triangle gives 3 remaining triangles at the next step: 1, 3, 9, 27, so the count at Step n is 3 to the power n.
2. Each remaining triangle also makes one new hole, and the old holes stay.
3. Holes: 0, 1, 1 + 3 = 4, 1 + 3 + 9 = 13, and so on.
4. At Step n the holes are 1 + 3 + 9 + ... up to 3 to the power (n − 1), which equals (3 to the power n, minus 1) divided by 2.
Answer: Remaining triangles: 3 to the power n. Holes: 1 + 3 + 9 + ... up to n terms, which is (3 to the power n, minus 1) divided by 2

content.text:
Figure it Out (sierpinski fractals, question 3): Find the area of the region remaining at the nth step in each of the shape sequences that lead to the Sierpinski fractals. Take the area of the starting square/triangle to be 1 sq. unit.
1. Carpet: each step keeps 8 of the 9 equal parts of every square, so the area is multiplied by 8/9.
2. After Step 2 the carpet has 8/9 × 8/9 = 64/81 square unit left.
3. Triangle: each step keeps 3 of the 4 equal parts, so the area is multiplied by 3/4.
4. After Step 2 the triangle has 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16 square unit left.
Answer: Carpet: (8/9) to the power n square unit. Triangle: (3/4) to the power n square unit. Both shrink towards 0

concepts.concept_name: The bump rule of the Koch Snowflake

content.text:
The Koch Snowflake is another fractal, named after the Swedish mathematician Von Koch, who first described it in 1904. We have already encountered this fractal in Grade 6, Ganita Prakash.
To generate it, we start with an equilateral triangle. Each side is (i) divided into 3 equal parts, and (ii) an equilateral triangle is raised over the middle part, and then the middle part is removed.
Effectively, each side gets replaced by a 'bump' shaped structure.
This procedure is repeated on the sides of the new resulting shape, and so on.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a triangle has 3 sides. After every side gets a bump, how many sides are there?
2. One side becomes 4 shorter sides: the two outer thirds and the two sides of the bump.
3. So 3 sides become 3 × 4 = 12 sides, each one third of the old length.
4. The perimeter changes from 3 to 12 × 1/3 = 4 when each starting side is 1 unit.

content.text:
Worked example: Start with an equilateral triangle of side 1 unit. Find the number of sides, the length of each side and the perimeter at Step 1 of the Koch Snowflake.
1. Each side is cut into 3 parts of 1/3 unit, and the middle part is replaced by two sides of a bump.
2. So each side becomes 4 sides: 3 × 4 = 12 sides.
3. Each side is 1/3 unit long.
4. Perimeter = 12 × 1/3 = 4 units.
Answer: 12 sides, each 1/3 unit, perimeter 4 units

concepts.concept_name: Fractals in temples, blankets and prints

content.text:
Fractals have also long been used in human-made art! Perhaps the oldest such fractals appear in the temples of India. An example occurs in the Kandariya Mahadev Temple in Khajuraho, Madhya Pradesh which was completed in around 1025 C.E.; there one sees a tall temple structure, which is made up of smaller copies of the full structure, on which there are even smaller copies of the same structure, and so on. Fractal-like patterns also occur in temples in Madurai, Hampi, Rameswaram, Varanasi, among many others.
Fractals are also common in traditional African cultures. For example, patterns on Nigerian Fulani wedding blankets often exhibit fractal structures.
In the blanket shown in the figure, there are diamond shaped patterns, inside of which there are smaller diamond shaped patterns, and so on.
The modern maestro of fractal art is undoubtedly the Dutch artist M.C. Escher. One famous example involving fractals is his work 'Smaller and Smaller', which exhibits the identical pattern of lizards but at smaller and smaller scales.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a diamond is drawn inside a bigger one by joining the midpoints of its sides. Does the inner diamond take more or less than half the area?
2. Joining the midpoints of a rhombus gives a shape with exactly half its area, because each corner cut off matches a piece left inside.
3. Repeating it gives a diamond pattern like the Fulani blankets, each shape half the one before.
4. The temple spire is built of smaller spires in the same way; Escher's lizards shrink ring by ring.

content.text:
Worked example: A diamond pattern has area 64 square cm. Each new shape is drawn by joining the midpoints of the sides of the one before. What is the area of the third shape inside?
1. Joining the midpoints keeps exactly half the area each time.
2. First shape inside: 64 ÷ 2 = 32 square cm.
3. Second: 32 ÷ 2 = 16 square cm.
4. Third: 16 ÷ 2 = 8 square cm.
Answer: 8 square cm

content.text:
Figure it Out (koch snowflake, question 1): Draw the initial few steps (at least till Step 2) of the shape sequence that leads to the Koch Snowflake.
1. Step 0: draw an equilateral triangle with sides of 9 units on dot paper so thirds are easy.
2. Step 1: on each side raise a bump on the middle third; a six pointed star with 12 sides appears.
3. Step 2: put a smaller bump on the middle third of each of the 12 sides.
Answer: Step 0 has 3 sides, Step 1 is a star with 12 sides, Step 2 has 48 sides

content.text:
Figure it Out (koch snowflake, question 2): Find the number of sides in the nth step of the shape sequence that leads to the Koch Snowflake.
1. Step 0 has 3 sides.
2. Each step turns every side into 4 sides, so the count is multiplied by 4.
3. Step 1: 3 × 4 = 12. Step 2: 12 × 4 = 48. Step 3: 48 × 4 = 192.
Answer: 3 × (4 to the power n) sides at Step n

content.text:
Figure it Out (koch snowflake, question 3): Find the perimeter of the shape at the nth step of the sequence. Take the starting equilateral triangle to have a sidelength of 1 unit.
1. At Step n there are 3 × (4 to the power n) sides.
2. Each step makes every side one third as long, so each side is 1/3 to the power n.
3. Step 1: 12 × 1/3 = 4. Step 2: 48 × 1/9 = 16/3.
4. Each step multiplies the perimeter by 4/3.
Answer: 3 × (4/3) to the power n units; the perimeter keeps growing

content.text:
4.2 Visualising Solids
Build it in Your Imagination
We will start this section by practising visualisation. For each prompt, feel free to talk to your partner, gesture, draw it in the air, but do not actually draw on paper!
My method is different. I do not rush into actual work. When I get an idea I start at once building it up in my imagination. I change the construction, make improvements, and operate the device entirely in my mind. (Nikolas Tesla, 1856 to 1943, the great Serbian-American engineer and inventor)
1. Picture your name, then read off the letters backwards. Make sure to do this by sight, not by sound, really see your name! Now try with your friend's name.
2. Cut off the four corners of an imaginary square, with each cut going between midpoints of adjacent edges. What shape is left over? How can you reassemble the four corners to make another square?

content.text:
1. Predict first: close your eyes and cut the four corners of a square from midpoint to midpoint. What shape is left, and is it bigger or smaller than the four corners put together?
2. The four cuts are equal and meet at right angles, so a smaller square is left, standing on a corner.
3. Each corner is a right triangle; turn the four triangles so their right angles meet at the centre and they form another square.
4. The two squares have the same area, each half of the starting square.

content.text:
Worked example: A square has side 4 cm. Its corners are cut off from midpoint to midpoint. Find the area of the square that is left and of the square made from the four corners.
1. The starting square has area 4 × 4 = 16 square cm.
2. Each corner triangle has two sides of 2 cm at a right angle: area 2 × 2 ÷ 2 = 2 square cm.
3. The four corners together: 4 × 2 = 8 square cm, and they fit together into a square.
4. The square left over: 16 − 8 = 8 square cm.
Answer: Both squares have area 8 square cm, half of the starting square

content.text:
1. Predict first: a triangle loses 3 corners and a square loses 4. How many sides does each shape left have, and are all its sides equal?
2. Each corner of the triangle cut at the thirds is a small equilateral triangle, so all 6 sides left are equal: a regular hexagon.
3. Each corner of the square cut at the thirds is a right triangle whose slanted side is longer than a third, so the octagon has two side lengths and is not regular.

content.text:
Worked example: Cut the corners at the thirds of an equilateral triangle of side 9 cm and of a square of side 9 cm. Find the side lengths of the shapes left.
1. Triangle: each side keeps its middle third of 9 ÷ 3 = 3 cm.
2. Each cut corner is an equilateral triangle of side 3 cm, so each cut edge is 3 cm: a regular hexagon of side 3 cm.
3. Square: each side keeps its middle third of 3 cm.
4. Each cut edge is the slanted side of a right triangle with sides 3 cm and 3 cm: √(3² + 3²) = √18, about 4.24 cm.
5. So the octagon has sides 3 cm and about 4.24 cm, and it is not regular.
Answer: A regular hexagon of side 3 cm; an octagon with sides 3 cm and about 4.24 cm, not regular

content.text:
When we see a solid object, we are really seeing its profile from a specific viewpoint. Depending on our viewpoint, the outline of this profile can vary dramatically!
Perhaps you've noticed interesting profiles of objects yourself, while taking a photograph or observing the shadow of an object? Or, maybe you've seen a cartoon in which a character bursts through a wall and leaves a hole shaped like their outline!
In previous classes, you've seen solids that are much simpler than an elephant or cat, such as cubes, spheres, cylinders, and cones. What would the profiles of these look like, from different viewpoints?
Can you describe a solid and a viewpoint that would result in each of the following cases? If it helps, you can imagine the solid passing through a wall like Tom did, and leaving a hole of the appropriate shape.
5. A solid whose profile has a square outline

1. Predict first: a tin can passes through a paper wall. What shape is the hole if it goes in lid first, and what if it goes in lying on its side?
2. Lid first: a circle. Lying on its side: a rectangle. One solid, two profiles.
3. A cube face on gives a square; a sphere from any side gives a circle; a cone seen from the side gives a triangle.

content.text:
Worked example: A tin can is a cylinder with radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. What profile does it show from directly above, and what from the side?
1. From directly above you see the round lid: a circle of radius 3 cm.
2. From the side you see the height and the width: a rectangle.
3. The width of the rectangle is the diameter, 2 × 3 = 6 cm, and its height is 10 cm.
Answer: A circle of radius 3 cm from above; a 6 cm by 10 cm rectangle from the side

1. Predict first: which everyday object looks like a trapezium from the side and a circle from above?
2. A bucket: its sides slope out, so from the side its outline is a trapezium; from above it is round.
3. Rectangle and circle: a cylinder. Circle and triangle: a cone. Rectangle and triangle: a tent shaped triangular prism. Pentagon and rectangle: a pentagonal prism, like a hut.
4. Each pair has more than one answer, so the solids are not unique.

Worked example: Give two different solids that each show a rectangular profile from one viewpoint and a triangular profile from another.
1. A tent shaped triangular prism: from the front a triangle, from the side a rectangle.
2. A square pyramid seen from the side gives a triangle, but from above it gives a square, which is a rectangle with equal sides.
3. So both a triangular prism and a square pyramid work, and there are more.
Answer: A triangular prism and a square pyramid, among others

content.text:
Worked example: A cylinder has radius 7 cm and height 14 cm. Picture it before you draw it: what profile does it show from the side, and what from directly above?
1. From the side you see its width and its height.
2. The width is the diameter: 2 × 7 = 14 cm, and the height is 14 cm.
3. Width and height are equal, so the side profile is a square of side 14 cm.
4. From directly above you see the round top: a circle of radius 7 cm.
Answer: A square of side 14 cm from the side and a circle of radius 7 cm from above

content.text:
Making Solids
Many basic solid shapes such as a cuboid, parallelopiped, cylinder, cone, prism, and pyramid can be made using foldable flat materials like paper, cardboard, and even metallic sheets! This is one of the methods for manufacturing hollow solids.
While discussing solids that contain plane surfaces in their boundaries, the notion of faces, edges and vertices serves a useful purpose.
Faces are the plane/flat surfaces of a solid that form its boundary. Edges are the line segments that form the sides of the faces, and vertices are the points at which the edges meet. For example, a cuboid or cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.

content.text:
1. Predict first: hold a matchbox. How many flat faces, straight edges and corners does it have?
2. 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices: 4 edges around the top, 4 around the bottom and 4 upright.
3. A triangular prism (like a tent) has 2 triangles and 3 rectangles.

content.text:
Worked example: Count the faces, edges and vertices of a triangular prism.
1. Faces: 2 triangles and 3 rectangles, so 2 + 3 = 5.
2. Edges: 3 on each triangle and 3 joining them, so 3 + 3 + 3 = 9.
3. Vertices: 3 on each triangle, so 3 + 3 = 6.
Answer: 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices

concepts.concept_name: Counting the parts of a prism

content.text:
There are multiple types of prisms and pyramids, whose names depend on the shapes of their faces.
Prism: A prism, in general, has two congruent polygons as opposite faces, with edges connecting the corresponding vertices of these polygons. All the other faces are parallelograms. Based on the shape of the congruent polygons, prisms may be called triangular prisms, pentagonal prisms, and so on.
If the congruent polygons of a prism have 10 sides, how many faces, edges and vertices does the prism have? What if the polygons have n sides?

content.text:
1. Predict first: a prism on a 10 sided polygon. How many side faces does it need?
2. One parallelogram face for each side of the polygon: 10, plus the 2 polygons.
3. Edges: 10 on the top polygon, 10 on the bottom, 10 joining them. Vertices: 10 on each polygon.
4. For n sides: n + 2 faces, 3n edges, 2n vertices.

content.text:
Worked example: A prism has two congruent 10 sided polygons as opposite faces. Find its faces, edges and vertices.
1. Faces: 10 parallelograms and 2 polygons, 10 + 2 = 12.
2. Edges: 10 + 10 + 10 = 30.
3. Vertices: 10 + 10 = 20.
Answer: 12 faces, 30 edges, 20 vertices; for n sides, n + 2 faces, 3n edges and 2n vertices

content.text:
Pyramids: A pyramid, in general, has a polygonal base and a point outside it, and edges connect the point with each of the vertices of the base. Based on the shape of the base, pyramids may be called triangular pyramids, square pyramids, pentagonal pyramids, and so on. A triangular pyramid is also known as a tetrahedron.
If the base of a pyramid has 10 sides, how many faces, edges and vertices does the pyramid have? What if the base is an n-sided polygon?

content.text:
1. Predict first: a pyramid and a prism both on a 10 sided polygon. Which has more edges?
2. The pyramid has one triangle on each side of the base: 10 triangles plus the base.
3. Edges: 10 around the base and 10 up to the apex. Vertices: 10 on the base and the apex.
4. For n sides: n + 1 faces, 2n edges, n + 1 vertices.

concepts.concept_name: Practice: count faces, edges and vertices

content.text:
Worked example: A gift box is a prism on an octagon, and its lid is a pyramid on the same octagon. Find the faces, edges and vertices of each.
1. Prism, n = 8: faces 8 + 2 = 10, edges 3 × 8 = 24, vertices 2 × 8 = 16.
2. Pyramid, n = 8: faces 8 + 1 = 9, edges 2 × 8 = 16, vertices 8 + 1 = 9.
3. Check the prism: faces + vertices − edges = 10 + 16 − 24 = 2.
4. Check the pyramid: 9 + 9 − 16 = 2.
Answer: Octagonal prism: 10 faces, 24 edges, 16 vertices; octagonal pyramid: 9 faces, 16 edges, 9 vertices

tool_config.title: Solid Parts Counter: Prisms and Pyramids
tool_config.idea: A prism on an n sided polygon has n plus 2 faces, 3n edges and 2n vertices, while a pyramid on the same polygon has n plus 1 faces, 2n edges and n plus 1 vertices. Changing n shows how each count depends on the number of sides of the base.
tool_config.screen: A 3D prism or pyramid that can be turned, a switch between Prism and Pyramid, a slider for the number of sides n of the base from 3 to 12, tap to highlight a face, an edge or a vertex, and a counter panel for faces, edges and vertices.
student_does: Choose a solid and a number of sides, and predict the faces, edges and vertices before reading the counter.
Tap the faces, edges and vertices one by one to count them on the solid.
Change n and watch which counts change and by how much.
Write the rule for each count in terms of n.
challenges: Triangular prism: find the faces, edges and vertices.
Square pyramid: find the faces, edges and vertices.
Pentagonal prism: find the faces, edges and vertices.
Hexagonal pyramid: find the faces, edges and vertices.
A prism on a 12 sided polygon: find the faces, edges and vertices.
A prism and a pyramid both have a 9 sided base: which has more edges, and what is faces plus vertices minus edges for each?
A pyramid has 24 edges: how many sides does its base have?
feedback: A prism count given for a pyramid is shown with the two solids side by side, with the extra edges and vertices highlighted.
A count that misses the base faces highlights the two bases of the prism, or the single base of the pyramid.
A rule that does not fit a second value of n is tested on the solid with that n.
tool_config.done_when: All seven cards are answered with the counts matching the counter.

hint_ladder.text: Which polygon is the base, and how many sides does it have?
Count the side faces first: there is one for every side of the base.
For a prism add the two bases; for a pyramid add one base. Count edges and vertices on the base polygon, then on the rest of the solid.
The counts are shown on the solid with their rule in n and the next card follows.

concepts.concept_name: What is a net? Folding the cross

content.text:
Now we will see how to make different solids using a foldable flat surface such as paper, cardboard, etc.
The basic idea is to create a shape on a flat surface that can be folded into the solid. Such a shape is called a net. In other words, a net is obtained by 'unfolding' a solid onto a plane.
What is a net of a cube? Fig. 4.1 is a net of a cube.
Visualise how it can be folded to form a cube.
Practical Aspects of Using a Net: To make an actual cube from its net, certain practical aspects have to be kept in mind. One is that the material used must have sufficient sturdiness for the cube to stand. The second aspect is that there should be some mechanism for attaching the faces together. If cardboard or a similar material is used, cello tape is one way to join the adjacent faces. For less sturdy materials, such as chart paper, it is useful to have extra 'flaps' on some of the faces that can be stuck to the adjacent faces.
However, when we talk about the net of a solid, we consider only the shape formed by unfolding the solid, and not the other supporting flaps that we may use to actually make the solid.
There are multiple possible nets one can use to build a cube.

content.text:
Worked example: A cross shaped net has a column of four squares A, B, C, D from top to bottom, and two squares L and R on either side of B. Fold it into a cube with B as the bottom. Which faces are opposite each other?
1. B is the bottom; A, C, L and R fold up as the four walls.
2. D is attached to C, so it folds over the top: D is opposite B.
3. A and C are on opposite sides of B, so they are opposite walls.
4. L and R are on opposite sides of B, so they are opposite walls too.
Answer: B and D, A and C, L and R are the pairs of opposite faces

concepts.concept_name: Will these six squares fold into a cube?

content.text:
1. Predict first: a row of four squares with both extra squares above the same end square. Will it fold into a cube?
2. The row of four wraps round to make four walls. One extra square becomes the lid.
3. The other extra square is attached to the lid, so it folds down onto a wall that is already there: two faces overlap and the bottom stays open.
4. With a row of four, one extra square must go above the row and one below.

content.text:
Worked example: Six squares: a row of four, one square above the first square of the row, and one more square to the left of that square. Is it a net of a cube?
1. The row of four folds round into four walls; call the first square the front.
2. The square above the front folds over as the lid.
3. The last square is attached to the left edge of the lid, so it folds down onto the left wall.
4. Two faces land on the left wall and the bottom is missing.
Answer: No, it is not a net of a cube

concepts.concept_name: Drawing a net of a cuboid

content.text:
1. Predict first: a cuboid has 6 faces. How many different sizes of rectangle does its net need?
2. Opposite faces are equal, so there are 3 pairs: length by breadth, length by height, breadth by height.
3. Draw a row of four walls whose heights match, then the top and bottom on the long edges.
4. Every pair of edges that will be glued together must have the same length.

content.text:
Worked example: Draw a net of a cuboid 4 cm by 2 cm by 1 cm and find the area of the net.
1. Rectangles needed: two of 4 cm by 2 cm, two of 4 cm by 1 cm, two of 2 cm by 1 cm.
2. Draw the walls in a row: 4 by 1, 2 by 1, 4 by 1, 2 by 1, all 1 cm tall.
3. Attach two 4 by 2 rectangles above and below a 4 by 1 wall as the top and bottom.
4. Area = 2 × (8 + 4 + 2) = 28 square cm.
Answer: A net of six rectangles with area 28 square cm

content.text:
Figure it Out (nets, question 1): Which of the following are the nets of a cube? First, try to answer by visualisation. Then, you may use cutouts and try. (i) two squares on top and a row of four below, joined only at the second square; (ii) a row of three on top and a row of three below, joined at one square; (iii) a staircase of 2, 2 and 2 squares; (iv) a row of four with one square above and one below the third square; (v) a row of four with two squares hanging in a column below the second square; (vi) a row of four with one square above the third square and one below the second square.
1. (i): the row of four makes the walls, one square becomes the lid, and the sixth square folds onto a wall: not a net.
2. (ii): the 3 and 3 staircase folds with no overlap: a net.
3. (iii): the 2, 2, 2 staircase folds with no overlap: a net.
4. (iv) and (vi): a row of four with one square above and one below: nets.
5. (v): both extra squares are below the row, so one lands on a wall: not a net.
Answer: (ii), (iii), (iv) and (vi) are nets of a cube; (i) and (v) are not

3. (iii): the 2, 2, 2 staircase folds with no overlap: a net.
4. (iv) and (vi): a row of four with one square above and one below: nets.
5. (v): both extra squares are below the row, so one lands on a wall: not a net.
Answer: (ii), (iii), (iv) and (vi) are nets of a cube; (i) and (v) are not
content.question: Which of the following are the nets of a cube? First, try to answer by visualisation. Then, you may use cutouts and try. (i) two squares on top and a row of four below, joined only at the second square; (ii) a row of three on top and a row of three below, joined at one square; (iii) a staircase of 2, 2 and 2 squares; (iv) a row of four with one square above and one below the third square; (v) a row of four with two squares hanging in a column below the second square; (vi) a row of four with one square above the third square and one below the second square.

(ii): the 3 and 3 staircase folds with no overlap: a net.
(iii): the 2, 2, 2 staircase folds with no overlap: a net.
(iv) and (vi): a row of four with one square above and one below: nets.
(v): both extra squares are below the row, so one lands on a wall: not a net.

content.text:
Figure it Out (nets, question 2): A cube has 11 possible net structures in total. In this count, two nets are considered the same if one can be obtained from the other by a rotation or a flip. Find all the 11 nets of a cube.
1. Row of four with one square above and one below: 6 nets (the extra squares above positions 1 to 4 and below positions 1 to 4, removing turns and flips).
2. Row of three in the middle: 3 nets with 1 square on one side and 2 on the other, and 1 net of two rows of three.
3. The staircase of 2, 2 and 2: 1 net.
4. Count: 6 + 4 + 1 = 11.
Answer: 6 nets with a row of four, 4 with a longest row of three, and 1 staircase: 11 in all

content.text:
Figure it Out (nets, question 3): Draw a net of a cuboid having sidelengths: (i) 5 cm, 3 cm, and 1 cm (ii) 6 cm, 3 cm, and 2 cm
1. (i): two rectangles 5 by 3, two 5 by 1, two 3 by 1; walls in a row 5, 3, 5, 3 long and 1 cm tall, with 5 by 3 rectangles above and below a 5 cm wall.
2. Area of net (i) = 2 × (15 + 5 + 3) = 46 square cm.
3. (ii): two rectangles 6 by 3, two 6 by 2, two 3 by 2; walls 6, 3, 6, 3 long and 2 cm tall, with 6 by 3 rectangles above and below a 6 cm wall.
4. Area of net (ii) = 2 × (18 + 12 + 6) = 72 square cm.
Answer: Nets of six rectangles in three equal pairs, with areas 46 square cm and 72 square cm

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students describe a net as a solid unfolded onto a plane, visualise folding the cross shaped net into a cube and name the pairs of opposite faces.
Students test an arrangement of six squares by folding it in the mind, find where two faces would overlap, and decide whether it is a net of a cube.
Students draw a net of a cuboid with given side lengths by pairing equal rectangles, and check it with the total area.
Students decide which arrangements of six squares fold into a cube, collect the 11 nets of a cube and draw nets of cuboids with given side lengths.

concepts.concept_name: Nets of a tetrahedron, a pyramid and a prism

content.text:
Let us find out the nets of other solids.
A tetrahedron whose faces are equilateral triangles is called a regular tetrahedron.
What is a net of a regular tetrahedron? Which of the following are nets of a regular tetrahedron?
Are there any other possible nets? A regular tetrahedron has only 2 possible nets.
Draw a net with appropriate measurements that can be folded into a regular tetrahedron. Verify if it works by making an actual cutout.
Draw a net with appropriate measurements that can be folded into a square pyramid. Verify if it works by making an actual cutout.
Draw a net with appropriate measurements that can be folded into a triangular prism. Verify that it works by making an actual cutout.

1. Predict first: four triangles all meet at one point in a shape. Can it fold into a tetrahedron?
2. Only three faces meet at each corner of a tetrahedron, so four triangles around one point overlap.
3. The two nets are a large triangle cut into four, and a strip of four triangles.
4. A square pyramid net: a square with a triangle on each side. A triangular prism net: three rectangles in a row with a triangle on two opposite long edges.

content.text:
Worked example: Four shapes are made of equilateral triangles: a large triangle of 4, four triangles that all meet at one point, a straight strip of 4, and a strip of 4 with a fifth triangle below. Which are nets of a regular tetrahedron?
1. A regular tetrahedron has 4 faces with 3 meeting at each corner.
2. The large triangle of 4 folds its three corners up to meet: a net.
3. Four triangles around one point would put 4 faces at one corner: not a net.
4. The straight strip of 4 folds into a tetrahedron: a net.
5. The last shape has 5 triangles, one too many: not a net.
Answer: Only the large triangle and the straight strip of 4

content.text:
Worked example: A cylinder has radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. Find the sides of the rectangle in its net, using π as 22/7.
1. The long side wraps once round the base: the circumference 2 × π × 7.
2. 2 × 22/7 × 7 = 44 cm.
3. The short side is the height, 10 cm.
Answer: A 44 cm by 10 cm rectangle with two circles of radius 7 cm

content.text:
1. Predict first: a birthday cap is slit along a line from the tip and laid flat. Is the flat shape a triangle?
2. Every point of the rim is the slant length l from the tip, so the rim becomes an arc of a circle of radius l with centre at the tip: a sector.
3. The arc is as long as the circumference of the base.
4. If the tip is not the centre of the boundary, the cone leans to one side: a slanted (oblique) cone.

content.text:
Worked example: A cone has base radius 5 cm and slant length 10 cm. What fraction of a full circle of radius 10 cm is its unrolled curved surface?
1. The arc of the sector equals the base circumference: 2 × π × 5 = 10π cm.
2. A full circle of radius 10 cm has circumference 2 × π × 10 = 20π cm.
3. Fraction = 10π ÷ 20π = 1/2.
Answer: Half of the circle: a semicircle of radius 10 cm

content.text:
Here is a solid called the octahedron, made by joining two square pyramids at their square bases.
Can you visualise its net? This is one of its nets. Taking all the triangles in the net to be equilateral, make a cutout of the net and fold it to form an octahedron.
As in the case of cubes, an octahedron too has 11 different nets.
So far, we have seen solids whose faces are all equilateral triangles (regular tetrahedrons), and all squares (cubes). Does there exist a solid whose faces are all pentagons? Interestingly, the answer is yes! This solid is called a dodecahedron. This solid too can be made from a net! Mathematicians have been even able to determine exactly how many nets a dodecahedron has: 43,380.
Net of a sphere? Experiment and see if you can make a paper cutout that can perfectly wrap around a ball without leaving any wrinkles, gaps or overlaps.

content.text:
Worked example: An octahedron is two square pyramids joined at their square bases. Plan a net for it with equilateral triangles, and count its faces, edges and vertices.
1. Each pyramid gives 4 triangles around its apex, so the octahedron has 4 + 4 = 8 faces.
2. Unfold the top 4 triangles as a fan around the top corner, and the bottom 4 as a fan around the bottom corner.
3. Join the two fans along one edge of the square, one fan on each side of it: 8 triangles with no overlap.
4. Edges: 4 round the square, 4 up to the top and 4 down to the bottom, so 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
5. Vertices: 4 on the square, the top and the bottom, so 4 + 1 + 1 = 6.
Answer: Two fans of 4 equilateral triangles joined along one edge; 8 faces, 12 edges and 6 vertices

For the cylinder, the long side is 2 times pi times the radius; for the cone, the sector fraction is the base radius divided by the slant length.
The net is shown with its measurements and a similar card follows.

media.instructions_for_student: A cylinder unrolls into two circles and a rectangle whose sides are the circumference of the base and the height. A cone unrolls into a circle and a sector of a circle whose radius is the slant length and whose arc is as long as the circumference of the base.

media.title: Which triangle shapes fold into a tetrahedron?
media.context: Exploring Some Geometric Themes. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Four shapes made of equal triangles are folded in the mind, with three faces at every corner of a regular tetrahedron. The board finds the two nets. Keeko's doubt is that any four triangles will fold into a tetrahedron.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: a regular tetrahedron has four triangle faces and three meet at each corner, so a net must fold with exactly three faces at every corner. Watch for students who count the four triangles and stop there.

media.title: What fraction of a circle is a cone's curved surface?
media.context: Exploring Some Geometric Themes. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A cone has base radius five centimetres and slant length ten centimetres. The board matches the curved edge of the flat piece with the distance round the base, then compares it with the full circle of radius ten centimetres. Keeko's doubt is that it is a quarter of the circle.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: the curved edge of the unrolled cone equals the distance round its base, so the fraction of the circle is the curved edge divided by the full circle's edge. Watch for students who guess the fraction by halving the radius twice.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

video_script.substitution: base radius 5 cm, slant length 10 cm; curved edge 2 x pi x 5 = 10 pi; full circle of radius 10 cm has circumference 2 x pi x 10 = 20 pi; fraction 10 pi / 20 pi = 1/2.
video_script.anchor: the cone of the book opened out flat into a piece of a circle of radius 10 cm
video_script.wrong_answer: it is a quarter of the circle
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko halves the radius, five is half of ten, then halves again to get a quarter; the fraction comes from comparing the curved edge with the full circle, which gives a half, so the doubt is struck.

final_answer.value: Half of the circle: a semicircle of radius 10 cm
final_answer.spoken: half of the circle, a semicircle of radius ten centimetres

maths_rules: the flat piece is part of a circle whose radius is the slant length, 10 cm
its curved edge wraps once round the base: 2 x pi x 5 = 10 pi
the full circle of radius 10 cm has circumference 2 x pi x 10 = 20 pi
fraction = 10 pi divided by 20 pi = 1/2
the same result as base radius divided by slant length: 5 / 10 = 1/2
wrong idea: halving 5 to 10 and then halving again gives 1/4, which does not match the lengths

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students decide which arrangements of four equilateral triangles fold into a regular tetrahedron and plan nets of a square pyramid and a triangular prism with measurements.
Students explain that the net of a cylinder is two circles and a rectangle whose sides are the circumference of the base and the height, and find these sides.

content.text:
Shortest Paths on a Cube
We know that on a plane, the shortest path between two points is the straight line between them. Now, what is the shortest path between two points on the surface of a cuboid, if we are allowed to travel only along its surface?
Let us imagine a hungry ant living on the surface of a cuboid. To its good fortune, there is a laddu on the surface. Laddu at the centre of the top face, ant at the centre of the side face.
What is the shortest path for the ant to reach the laddu?
If we think that a certain path is the shortest, how can we be sure that it truly is, among all the infinite possibilities? For example, are either of these the shortest path? [Hint: Draw the net and see how these paths appear on the net.]
A path on the surface of the cuboid can be transformed to a path of the same length on the net. Conversely, every path on the net transforms to a path of the same length on the cuboid.
In the first case, the path marked on the cuboid is the shortest since it transforms to a straight line between the ant and laddu on the net, which is the shortest path between them.
Thus, by using a net, we convert the problem of finding the shortest path on a cuboid to the problem of finding the shortest path on the net.

content.text:
1. Predict first: the ant is at the centre of a side face and the laddu at the centre of the top face. Should the ant walk straight up and across, or cut diagonally?
2. Unfold the top face so it lies flat beside the side face. Now both are on one flat piece.
3. The straight line between them on the net is the shortest; fold it back and it goes straight up and straight across the middle.
4. Any other path becomes a bent line on the net, which is longer.

content.text:
Worked example: A cube has side 4 cm. An ant is at the centre of a side face and a laddu at the centre of the top face. Find the length of the shortest path.
1. Unfold the top face so it sits flat above the side face.
2. The ant is 2 cm below the shared edge and the laddu is 2 cm beyond it, on the same straight line.
3. Shortest path = 2 + 2 = 4 cm.
Answer: 4 cm, straight up the middle of the side face and across to the centre of the top

content.text:
Worked example: A cube has side 6 cm. An ant is at the centre of the front face, and a laddu at the middle of the edge between the top face and the right face. Find the shortest path.
1. Unfold the right face so it lies flat beside the front face.
2. From the ant, the laddu is now 3 + 3 = 6 cm across and 3 cm up.
3. Shortest path = √(6² + 3²) = √45, about 6.71 cm.
4. Going up 3 cm and then across 6 cm would be 9 cm, which is longer.
Answer: About 6.71 cm, a slanted straight line on the net

Have we now completely analysed the problem of finding the shortest path between two points on a cuboid?
Find the shortest path between the ant and the laddu in the following case: a cuboid 8 cm by 4 cm by 4 cm, the ant at the centre of the end face, the laddu on the bottom edge, 2 cm from the end.
If we unfold the cuboid as before, we get a line segment between the ant and laddu going outside the net! Obviously, this does not correspond to any path on the cuboid. So what do we do now?
If the net is unfolded in the following way, then we get a path on the cuboid.
Thus, the way a cuboid is unfolded matters!

2. No. Part of the line runs over empty paper, so the ant cannot walk it.
3. Unfold the end face so it lies against the face that holds the laddu's edge. Now the straight line stays on the net.
4. Then measure it with a right triangle.

content.text:
Worked example: A cuboid is 8 cm by 4 cm by 4 cm. An ant is at the centre of a 4 cm by 4 cm end face. A laddu sits on a long bottom edge, 2 cm from that end. Find the shortest path.
1. Unfold the end face flat against the long face that meets the laddu's edge.
2. On this net the ant is 2 cm into the end face and 2 cm from the bottom edge line.
3. The laddu is 2 cm on the other side of the fold, on the bottom edge line.
4. So the line goes 2 + 2 = 4 cm along and 2 cm across.
5. Shortest path = √(4² + 2²) = √20, about 4.47 cm.
Answer: About 4.47 cm

concepts.concept_name: A trickier box: 40 cm beats 42 cm

content.text:
Now we will look at a trickier case. What is the length of the shortest path between the ant and the laddu? The box is 30 cm by 12 cm by 12 cm; the laddu is stuck to the back of the box, 1 cm from the bottom, and the ant is 1 cm from the top of the opposite end, both on the middle line.
Here are some of the ways of unfolding the cuboid.
In the second case, the distance d between the ant and the laddu can be calculated using the Baudhayana Theorem, since we have a right triangle here. d² = 24² + 32², d = √1600 = 40 cm.
We see that in each of these unfoldings, the lengths of the line segments between the ant and the laddu are different! So we have to carefully list all the possible different unfoldings to find the answer!

We see that in each of these unfoldings, the lengths of the line segments between the ant and the laddu are different! So we have to carefully list all the possible different unfoldings to find the answer!

content.text:
1. Predict first: the ant walks down its end, along the floor and up the far end. Can a slanted route over more faces be shorter?
2. The direct route: 11 cm down, 30 cm along, 1 cm up: 11 + 30 + 1 = 42 cm.
3. A slanted unfolding crosses five faces, but on the net it is the long side of a right triangle with sides 24 cm and 32 cm.
4. 24² + 32² = 1600 and √1600 = 40, so the slanted path is shorter.

content.text:
Worked example: For the 30 cm by 12 cm by 12 cm box, compare the 42 cm route with the slanted unfolding whose right triangle has sides 24 cm and 32 cm.
1. Straight route: 11 + 30 + 1 = 42 cm.
2. Slanted route: d² = 24² + 32² = 576 + 1024 = 1600.
3. d = √1600 = 40 cm.
4. 40 cm is less than 42 cm.
Answer: The slanted route of 40 cm is shorter than 42 cm

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students unfold the faces an ant must cross onto one plane and use a straight line on the net to find and justify the shortest path.
Students find the shortest path from the centre of a face to the middle of an edge that does not touch that face by drawing a slanted straight line on the net.
Students find that one unfolding can put the straight line outside the net, choose an unfolding that gives a real path, and compute its length.
Students compare two unfoldings of a 30 cm by 12 cm by 12 cm box, compute each path with the Baudhayana theorem where needed, and choose the shorter.
Students place an ant and a laddu on a box, unfold it in different ways, reject lines that leave the net, and measure each straight line to choose the shortest.

modules.module_summary: Projections of points, lines, flat shapes and solids; front, top and side views; shadows as projections and the fact that parallel lines stay parallel; the isometric projection of a cube and drawing solids on an isometric grid, ending with impossible figures and a closing summary.

concepts.concept_name: Projecting a point and a line

content.text:
Projections
The net of a solid (when it exists) is one way of representing a solid on the plane. But it can be difficult to visualise the solid from the net, without physically cutting out the net and folding it up.
Another way to represent a solid is by looking at the projections of all its points on a plane. This idea is closely related to the profile of a solid from a specific viewpoint, which we discussed earlier.
Consider a point P in space, and a plane M. Imagine a line from P intersecting the plane M at a point O. We say that OP is perpendicular to the plane if for any line OX on the plane, angle POX = 90°. In this case, we say that point O is the projection of point P on the plane. The projections of all the points of an object together form the projection of the object on the plane.
Let us visualise the projection of a line.
What happens to the length of a line in its projection? Let l be the actual length of the line and p be the length of its projection. Draw AE perpendicular to BC. AECD is a rectangle (why?). So, AE = DC = p. Also, angle AEB = 90°.
Can you now compare the lengths p and l? When is the length of the projected line equal to its actual length?

content.text:
1. Predict first: a pencil is held slanting above a table. Is its projection on the table longer, shorter or the same length as the pencil?
2. Drop a perpendicular from each end of the pencil to the table; the feet join to give the projection.
3. Slide the projection up to the lower end: the pencil, the projection and the height difference make a right triangle, and the pencil is its longest side.
4. So the projection is shorter, and equal only when the pencil lies parallel to the table.

4. So the projection is shorter, and equal only when the pencil lies parallel to the table.

content.text:
Worked example: A stick 5 cm long is held above a table so that one end is 3 cm higher than the other. How long is its projection on the table?
1. The stick, its projection and the height difference make a right triangle.
2. The stick is the longest side, 5 cm; the height difference is 3 cm.
3. Projection = √(5² − 3²) = √16 = 4 cm.
Answer: 4 cm, shorter than the stick

content.text:
1. Predict first: a square card is tilted above the floor. Can its projection be a trapezium?
2. Flat: a square. Tilted about one side: a rectangle. Tilted about a diagonal: a rhombus. Standing on edge: a line segment.
3. Opposite sides of a parallelogram are parallel and equal, and their projections stay parallel and equal, so the projection is a parallelogram (or a line), never a trapezium.
4. A regular polygon projects side by side: opposite parallel sides stay parallel, but the polygon can look squashed.

content.text:
Worked example: A square card of side 5 cm is tilted about one of its sides so that the opposite side is 3 cm higher. What is its projection on the floor?
1. The two sides parallel to the floor keep their length of 5 cm.
2. Each of the other two sides is 5 cm long and rises 3 cm, so it projects to √(5² − 3²) = 4 cm.
3. Parallel sides stay parallel, and the angles at the hinge stay right angles.
Answer: A rectangle 5 cm by 4 cm

content.text:
1. Predict first: a cone standing on its base is projected onto the floor. Can a different solid give the very same shape?
2. The cone's projection on the floor is a circle; a cylinder of the same radius also gives that circle, and so does a ball.
3. A cube resting on a face projects to a square; a tall cuboid with the same square base gives the same square.
4. One projection cannot tell us the object, so we will need more than one.

content.text:
Worked example: A cone standing on its base has base radius 4 cm. Name three different solids whose projection on the floor is the same circle.
1. The cone's projection on the floor is a circle of radius 4 cm.
2. A cylinder standing upright with radius 4 cm gives the same circle.
3. A ball of radius 4 cm and a bowl with rim radius 4 cm give it too.
Answer: A cylinder, a ball and a bowl, each with radius 4 cm

content.text:
Worked example: A rod 13 cm long is held above a table so that one end is 5 cm higher than the other. Predict the length of its projection, and say when the projection would be 13 cm.
1. The rod, its projection and the height difference make a right triangle with the rod as the longest side.
2. Projection = √(13² − 5²) = √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12 cm.
3. The projection equals 13 cm only when the rod is held parallel to the table.
Answer: 12 cm; it would be 13 cm only with the rod parallel to the table

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students find the projection of a point as the foot of the perpendicular, and use a right triangle to show that a projected line is never longer than the line.

Students describe the projections of a square in different orientations, explain why the projection of a parallelogram is always a parallelogram or a line, and build the projection of a polygon from its sides.

Students describe the projections of a cube and a cone, see that a projection is the shape of the hole left when an object passes straight through a plane, and find different objects with the same projection.
Students predict the projections of sticks, cards and solids held in different positions, check them with a torch or by looking straight down, and find a second object with each projection.

content.text:
For this reason, we often take three mutually perpendicular projections of an object. As shown in the figure, we consider a plane in front of the object called the vertical plane, a plane below the object called the horizontal plane and a plane to the side of the object called the side plane.
We give names to the projections on these three planes based on the directions from which the object is viewed. The projection on the vertical plane is called the front view, on the horizontal plane the top view and on the side plane the side view. These projections formalise the notion of profiles that we explored in an earlier section.
Let us see what these projections are for the objects shown in Fig. 4.6, when the planes shown are taken to be vertical planes. Projections of the different lines in Fig. 4.6. Projections of the different cuboids in Fig. 4.6.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a glass of water stands on the table. Which of its three views is a circle?

Worked example: A cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 8 cm stands on its base. Draw its front, top and side views.

3. Side view: the same as the front, a 6 cm by 8 cm rectangle.
Answer: Front and side views are 6 cm by 8 cm rectangles; the top view is a circle of radius 3 cm

content.text:
Figure it Out (views of solids, question 1): Observe the front view, top view and side view of the different lines in Fig. 4.6. Is there any relation between their lengths?
1. Each view is a projection, so no view is longer than the line itself.
2. A view shows the full length only when the line is parallel to that plane.
3. If a line goes a cm along, b cm deep and c cm up, the views have squared lengths a² + c², a² + b² and b² + c².
4. Adding these gives twice a² + b² + c², which is twice the square of the line's length.
Answer: No view is longer than the line; the squares of the three view lengths add up to twice the square of the line's length

content.text:
Figure it Out (views of solids, question 2): Find the front view, top view and side view of each of the following solids, fixing its orientation with respect to the vertical, horizontal and side planes: cube, cuboid, parallelepiped, cylinder, cone, prism, and pyramid.
1. Cube on a face: three squares.
2. Cuboid on a face: three rectangles.
3. Parallelepiped leaning forward: a parallelogram from the side, rectangles from the front and top.
4. Cylinder standing: rectangle, circle, rectangle.
5. Cone standing: triangle from the front and side, a circle with its centre point from the top.
6. Triangular prism with its triangle facing front: a triangle from the front, rectangles from the top and side.
7. Square pyramid standing: triangles from the front and side, a square with both diagonals from the top.
Answer: Cube: squares; cuboid: rectangles; cylinder: rectangle, circle, rectangle; cone: triangle, circle, triangle; prism: triangle and rectangles; pyramid: triangles and a square with diagonals

content.text:
Figure it Out (views of solids, question 3): Match each of the following objects with its projections: a jug, a funnel, a hammer, a car, a slide, a chair, a ceiling fan and a pressure cooker, each with a front, a top and a side view.
1. Jug: from the top a circle with a spout and a handle sticking out.
2. Funnel: front and side views are funnel shapes; from the top a circle with a dot at the centre.
3. Hammer: a long handle with the head seen end on from one side.
4. Car: a long rectangle from the top and a car profile from the side.
5. Slide: a ladder and a ramp in the side view.
6. Chair: a seat square from the top and a chair profile from the side.
7. Ceiling fan: blades seen edge on from the front and side, three blades from the top.
8. Pressure cooker: a pot with a handle from the front, a circle with a handle from the top.
Answer: Match each object by its most telling view, such as the circle with spout and handle for the jug and three blades from the top for the fan

media.title: How are the lengths of a line's three views related?
media.context: Exploring Some Geometric Themes. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A line goes some distance along, some deep and some up. The board finds the length of its front, top and side views, compares each with the line, and adds their squares. The relation is that no view is longer than the line and the three squares add up to twice the square of the line.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: each view keeps two of the three directions of the line, so its square is the sum of two of the three squares. Watch for students who think a view can be longer than the line.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; when the video says think and tell, say your answer.

video_script.why: The child relates the lengths of the three views of a line by looking from each direction as for the cylinder, because each view keeps two of the line's three directions.
video_script.substitution: line goes a along, b deep, c up; front view squared = a x a + c x c; top view squared = a x a + b x b; side view squared = b x b + c x c; line squared = a x a + b x b + c x c; sum of the three squares = 2 x (a x a + b x b + c x c) = 2 x line squared.
video_script.anchor: a slanted line in a box with its front, top and side views drawn as three lines on the three walls
video_script.payoff_line: No view is longer than the line. The squares of the three view lengths add up to twice the square of the line's length

final_answer.value: No view is longer than the line; the squares of the three view lengths add up to twice the square of the line's length

hold_back: No view is longer than the line; the squares of the three view lengths add up to twice the square of the line's length
maths_rules: the front view keeps along and up, the top view keeps along and deep, the side view keeps deep and up
front view squared = a x a + c x c; top view squared = a x a + b x b; side view squared = b x b + c x c
the top view lies flat and the line rises c above its end, a right triangle: line squared = a x a + b x b + c x c
each view square is the line square with one of the three squares missing, so no view is longer than the line
a view is as long as the line only when the missing direction is 0, that is, when the line is parallel to that plane
sum of the three view squares = 2 x (a x a + b x b + c x c) = 2 x line squared
check: a line running only along has front view and top view equal to the line and a side view of length 0; line squared + line squared + 0 = 2 x line squared

narration: <bookmark mark='front'/>Step one, find the length of each view. The front view keeps along and up, so its square is along squared plus up squared.
<bookmark mark='top'/>The top view keeps along and deep, so its square is along squared plus deep squared.
<bookmark mark='side'/>The side view keeps deep and up, so its square is deep squared plus up squared.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: the top view lies flat and the line rises c above its end; line squared = (a x a + b x b) + c x c

marks.tri: the line, its top view and the rise c are drawn as a right triangle
marks.sum: the working line squared = a x a + b x b + c x c is written

narration: <bookmark mark='tri'/>Step two, find the line's own length. The top view lies flat, and the line rises up from its end. They make a right triangle.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>The square of the line is the square of the top view plus up squared. That is along squared plus deep squared plus up squared.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: each view squared is the line squared with one square missing, so each view is at most as long as the line

marks.miss: in each view, one of the three squares is crossed out
marks.equal: a view equals the line only when the crossed out direction is 0, with the line parallel to that plane

narration: <bookmark mark='miss'/>Step three, compare each view with the line. Each view square has one of the three squares missing, so no view is longer than the line.
<bookmark mark='equal'/>A view is as long as the line only when the missing direction is zero. That is when the line is parallel to that plane.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: (a x a + c x c) + (a x a + b x b) + (b x b + c x c) = 2 x (a x a + b x b + c x c) = 2 x line squared

marks.add: the three view squares are added
marks.twice: each of the three squares appears twice, so the total is written as 2 times the line squared

beats.colours: three colours, one for each view
narration: <bookmark mark='add'/>Step four, add the squares of the three views.
<bookmark mark='twice'/>Along squared, deep squared and up squared each appear twice. The total is twice the line's square.

beats.on_screen: Check: a line that runs only along: front view and top view equal the line, side view is a dot; line squared + line squared + 0 = 2 x line squared

marks.flat: a line lying flat and running only along is drawn in the box
marks.dot: its front view and top view are as long as the line and its side view is a dot
marks.total: the three squares are added to line squared + line squared + 0

narration: <bookmark mark='flat'/>Step five, check with a line that runs only along.
<bookmark mark='dot'/>Its front view and top view are as long as the line. Its side view is a dot.
<bookmark mark='total'/>The squares add up to the line's square, twice over, and nothing more. The rule holds.

beats.on_screen: Answer: No view is longer than the line; the squares of the three view lengths add up to twice the square of the line's length
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>No view is longer than the line. The squares of the three view lengths add up to twice the square of the line's length.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students describe the vertical, horizontal and side planes and draw the front, top and side views of a cylinder.
Students draw the three views of a stack of identical cubes by looking along each direction and showing one square for every column seen.
Students compare the views of different lines, draw the three views of common solids, and match everyday objects with their front, top and side views.

media.title: What are the three views of seven solids?
media.context: Exploring Some Geometric Themes. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Seven solids, a cube, a cuboid, a parallelepiped, a cylinder, a cone, a prism and a pyramid, are each placed on a face or a base. The board looks at each from the front, from above and from the side and names the shape of each view.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: each view is the outline the eye meets from one direction, so fix the way the solid stands and look three times. Watch for students who give the cone a triangle from above.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; when the video says think and tell, say your answer.

content.text:
Shadows
Place an object in front of a plane, such as a wall of your room. Shine a torch light on the object in a direction perpendicular to the wall. What do you see?
We will see that the shape of the shadow on a plane is quite similar to the shape of the projection on that plane! However the shadow may be scaled up, stretched, or even distorted slightly, depending on how the object is held.
Observe what happens to the size of the shadow as you vary the distance between your torch and your object. Why does this happen?
Now, imagine your torch is extremely powerful and will continue casting a shadow of the object on the wall, no matter how far back you move it.
If this imaginary torch always points in a direction perpendicular to the wall, then, as the distance between the torch and the object increases, the shadow of the object will become indistinguishable from the projection of the object to the wall plane!
Although this experiment may sound fanciful, you have encountered one such extremely powerful and distant torch before, namely, the Sun! Indeed, when sunlight is perpendicular to a plane, the shadows it casts on that plane are indistinguishable from projections!

content.text:
1. Predict first: you move a torch away from a toy in front of a wall. Does the shadow grow or shrink?
2. Light spreads out from the torch, so the shadow is larger than the toy.
3. Moving the torch back makes the rays nearly parallel, and the shadow shrinks towards the toy's own size.
4. The Sun is so far away that its rays are parallel: its shadow on a wall it shines straight at is the projection.

content.text:
Worked example: A toy 10 cm tall stands 50 cm in front of a wall. A torch shines straight at the wall from 50 cm in front of the toy. How tall is the shadow? What if the torch is moved to 150 cm in front of the toy?
1. The rays spread from the torch, so the shadow and the toy make similar triangles.
2. Torch to wall is 50 + 50 = 100 cm, twice the torch to toy distance.
3. Shadow = 10 × 100 ÷ 50 = 20 cm.
4. With the torch at 150 cm, torch to wall is 150 + 50 = 200 cm.
5. Shadow = 10 × 200 ÷ 150 ≈ 13.3 cm, closer to the toy's 10 cm.
Answer: 20 cm, then about 13.3 cm: the farther the torch, the closer the shadow is to the projection

content.text:
Earlier we asked what the projection of a parallelogram might look like. You can now physically answer this question by making a cutout of a parallelogram and viewing its shadows under sunlight. No matter how you orient the parallelogram, you will see that the shadow remains a parallelogram!
More generally, the projection of a pair of parallel lines will always remain parallel. This property is useful for drawing projections of objects.

content.text:
1. Predict first: turn a square card in the sun. Can its shadow ever be a trapezium?
2. Opposite sides of the card are parallel, and parallel lines cast parallel shadows, so the shadow is always a parallelogram, never a trapezium.
3. Tilt the card about a diagonal: that diagonal keeps its length and the other one shrinks, so the shadow is a rhombus.

content.text:
Worked example: A square card has diagonals of 10 cm. It is tilted in sunlight about one diagonal, so the other diagonal's shadow is 6 cm. What is the shadow, and how long is each side?
1. The diagonal on the hinge stays 10 cm; the other diagonal's shadow is 6 cm.
2. The shadows of the diagonals still cross at right angles at their midpoints, and opposite sides stay parallel.
3. So the shadow is a rhombus with diagonals 10 cm and 6 cm.
4. Each side = √(5² + 3²) = √34, about 5.83 cm.
Answer: A rhombus with sides of about 5.83 cm

content.text:
Figure it Out (shadows and views, question 1): Draw the top view, front view and the side view of each of the following combinations of identical cubes.
1. Look along each direction in turn: front, top, side.
2. Draw one square for every column of cubes seen; a column hidden behind another adds nothing.
3. Check: the front and top views share the same width, and the front and side views share the same height.
Answer: For each combination, one square per visible column in each direction, with matching widths and heights across the views

content.text:
Figure it Out (shadows and views, question 2): Imagine eight identical cubes, glued together along faces to form the letter C. (i) This looks like a C from the front. What does it look like from the side? From the top? (ii) Glue additional cubes to make a shape that looks like one letter from the front and another from the top. (iii) Now, can you glue even more cubes to make it look like three given letters from the front, top and side? (iv) Can you think of other letter combinations to make with a single combination of cubes in this manner?
1. The C is 4 cubes tall: a row of 3 on top, 1 cube on the left in each of the two middle rows, and a row of 3 at the bottom, 3 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 8.
2. From the side every row hides behind its first cube: a column of 4 squares, like the letter I.
3. From the top the rows stack under each other: a row of 3 squares.
4. For (ii) to (iv), add cubes behind the front letter so the top view spells the second letter, then check the side view.
Answer: (i) From the side a column of 4 squares, from the top a row of 3 squares; (ii) to (iv) are built by adding cubes behind the letter

content.text:
Figure it Out (shadows and views, question 3): Which solid corresponds to the given top view, front view, and side view?
1. A circle in one view and rectangles in the others: a cylinder.
2. A circle in one view and triangles in the others: a cone.
3. A triangle in one view and rectangles in the others: a triangular prism.
4. A square with diagonals and triangles: a square pyramid; three squares: a cube.
Answer: Read the most unusual view first, then check the other two against the solid

1. Start from the top view: place one column of cubes on each square.
2. Use the front view to set the tallest column in each line from left to right.
3. Use the side view to set the tallest column in each line from front to back.
4. Build it and check all three views.
Answer: Columns placed on the top view squares, with heights fixed by the front and side views

content.text:
Figure it Out (shadows and views, question 5): Find the number of cubes in this stack of identical cubes.
1. Read the stack as a staircase in a corner, with every visible cube resting on cubes below it.
2. Count by layers from the top: 1, then 3, then 6, then 10.
3. Total = 1 + 3 + 6 + 10 = 20.
Answer: 20 cubes, if every hidden place under a visible cube is filled

Figure it Out (shadows and views, question 6): What are the different shapes the projection of a cube can make under different orientations?

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students explain with similar triangles why a torch shadow shrinks towards the size of the object as the torch moves away, and why sunlight shadows match projections.
Students use sunlight shadows of a parallelogram cutout to see that parallel lines project to parallel lines, and use this to predict shadows of a square tilted in different ways.
Students draw and read the three views of stacks of identical cubes, build stacks that match given views, count cubes in a stack, and list the shapes a cube's projection can make.

concepts.concept_name: A cube on its corner: the regular hexagon

content.text:
Isometric Projections
In general we lose information when projecting a solid to a plane. But depending on the orientation of the solid, we can sometimes recover much of the information we've lost.
Let us consider an orientation of a cube in which the lengths of the projections of all the edges of the cube are equal. Such a projection is called the isometric projection of the cube. 'Isometric' means 'equal measure' in Greek.
Imagine balancing a cube perfectly on one of its corner vertices, and then projecting it down to the floor plane. This projection is isometric.
Construct a model of a cube and use your hands to keep it balanced on one corner vertex. Can you try to understand why all the projected edges have equal length?
The isometric representation of a cube is a regular hexagon. If the cube is made of glass, then all the edges would be visible.
This structure is the basis for isometric drawing! Tile the plane with hexagons and we get an isometric grid.
Isometric grids are widely used in engineering. They make it easy to draw projections of solids and to measure lengths along all the 3 primary directions, length, depth and height, as shown in Fig. 4.7.

content.text:
1. Predict first: balance a cube on one corner and look straight down. What outline do you see?
2. The cube looks the same after a turn of a third of a full turn about that corner, so its edges come in matching sets that all slope the same way: their projections are equal.
3. The outline is a regular hexagon, with three edges meeting at its centre.
4. Fit many such hexagons together and the lines form the isometric grid.

content.text:
Worked example: A glass cube balanced on a corner is projected onto the floor. How many of its 12 edges form the hexagon outline, and how many lie inside it?
1. The top and bottom corners both project to the centre of the hexagon.
2. The 3 edges at the top corner and the 3 at the bottom corner run from the centre outwards: 3 + 3 = 6 inside.
3. The remaining 12 − 6 = 6 edges form the outline.
4. All 12 projections have the same length, so the outline is a regular hexagon.
Answer: 6 edges make the regular hexagon and 6 run inside from its centre

concepts.concept_name: Drawing edge by edge on the grid

content.text:
Drawing on Isometric Grids
Have you played Tetris? There are five basic shapes in Tetris, corresponding to the different ways of arranging four squares. Imagine these are cubes, not squares. Draw each of these on your isometric paper (you can find it at the end of the book).
As seen in Fig. 4.7, there are three principal axes of the solid shape, which we will call the depth axis, length axis, and height axis. The edges of the grid appear in three different orientations. We will associate height to the vertical lines, and depth and length to the two slanting families.
While drawing on the grid, it may be useful to draw edge by edge, counting the number of units you want to go along a given axis. For example, you can draw a 1 × 1 × 1 cube as follows. How would you draw a 2 × 2 × 2 cube? Feel free to add shading, if it helps you visualise the solid.
The first tetris shape is a row of four cubes joined face-to-face. In order to draw this solid, you will need to choose an orientation for the row of four cubes.
Let's draw it oriented along the depth axis. You could draw it cube-by-cube, but in that case you may need to erase the lines that get hidden by additional cubes. (If you don't have an eraser, you can also draw faint lines initially, and then darken the visible ones later.)
You could also draw it all at once, by counting edges as you go.
Similarly, you could draw the shape oriented along the height axis or the length axis.

content.text:
Worked example: Draw a 2 by 2 by 2 cube on an isometric grid. How many units of line do its visible edges use?
1. A box seen in isometric shows 9 edges: 3 along height, 3 along length, 3 along depth.
2. Each edge of this cube is 2 units long.
3. Total = 9 × 2 = 18 units.
Answer: 18 units of line over 9 visible edges

content.text:
In your drawing, moving in the vertical direction on the isometric paper corresponds to moving along the height axis of the solid. Similarly, moving along the two slanting directions on the paper corresponds to moving along the length or depth axis respectively of the solid.
Why is this correspondence between directions on isometric paper and axes of the solid so effective for communicating the shape of the solid?
Earlier we observed that parallel lines project to parallel lines. This geometric fact ensures that the three families of parallel edges on the solid (corresponding to height, the length, and depth) project to three families of parallel edges on the isometric paper. Moreover, the isometric nature of the projection ensures that the projections of unit distances along the three axes are equal.
Can you try drawing the other tetris shapes on isometric paper?

content.text:
Worked example: Draw a cuboid 1 unit long, 2 units deep and 3 units tall on the grid. How many units of line do its visible edges use?
1. 3 visible edges along length, each 1 unit: 3 × 1 = 3.
2. 3 visible edges along depth, each 2 units: 3 × 2 = 6.
3. 3 visible edges along height, each 3 units: 3 × 3 = 9.
4. Total = 3 + 6 + 9 = 18 units.
Answer: 18 units of line
