content.text:
Figure it Out (isometric drawing, question 1): In addition to the 5 ways shown in Fig. 4.8, are there any additional ways of gluing four cubes together along faces? Can you visualise and draw these as well?
1. The 5 tetris shapes all lie flat.
2. Lift one cube out of the flat plane: an L of three cubes with a fourth cube on top of the corner cube gives the tripod, three arms meeting at a corner.
3. An S shape with one end lifted up gives a twisted screw, and its mirror image twists the other way.
4. So there are 3 more, 5 + 3 = 8 in all.
Answer: Yes: 3 more, the tripod and two mirror image screws, for 8 ways in all

1. Follow the path: every step seems to go down, yet the path returns to where it began.
2. Each small piece can be built, but the pieces cannot all join in real space.
3. On the isometric grid, points at different depths can land on the same spot, which hides the break.
Answer: Yes: the ball keeps going down yet comes back to its start, which is impossible in real space

content.text:
Figure it Out (isometric drawing, question 4): Observe this triangle. (i) Would it be possible to build a model out of actual cubes? What are the front, top, and side profiles of this impossible triangle? (ii) Recreate this on an isometric grid. (iii) Why does the illusion work?
1. (i) No: each corner looks like a right angle bend, but three such bends cannot close into a triangle in real space. A real model of rows of cubes looks right only from one viewpoint.
2. (ii) Draw each arm as a row of cubes along a grid direction and join the ends where they appear to meet.
3. (iii) An isometric drawing loses depth: a near end and a far end can project to the same point, so the eye joins them.
Answer: It cannot be built; the illusion works because the projection loses depth, so far and near ends appear to touch

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students describe the isometric projection of a cube balanced on a corner, explain why all its projected edges are equal, and see how tiling the hexagons gives the isometric grid.
Students draw a 1 by 1 by 1 cube, a 2 by 2 by 2 cube and a row of four cubes on an isometric grid by counting units along the height, length and depth directions.
Students explain that parallel edges of a solid stay parallel and unit lengths stay equal on the grid, and use this to draw a cuboid and the other tetris shapes.
Students find and draw all the ways of gluing four cubes, copy given figures on the isometric grid and explain what makes the impossible ball path and the impossible triangle impossible.

concepts.concept_name: What we found about shapes and solids

content.text:
Fractals are self-similar geometric objects found in nature and in art.
The Sierpinski Carpet, Sierpinski Gasket, and Koch Snowflake are some examples of mathematical fractals. They can be obtained by repeatedly applying certain geometric operations that generate a sequence of shapes approaching the fractal.
Cuboids, tetrahedrons, cylinders, cones, prisms, pyramids, and octahedrons are some of the solids that can be obtained by folding suitable nets.
The shortest path between two points on the surface of a cuboid can be found by using a suitable net of the cuboid.
Any object can be represented on a plane surface by using its projections on plane surfaces. For this purpose, we generally use the front view (projection on the vertical plane), top view (projection on the horizontal plane), and side view (projection on the side plane) of the object.
A cube can be oriented such that the lengths of all its edges in the projection are equal. Such a projection is called the isometric projection. Isometric projections of different solids can be drawn using isometric grid paper.

content.text:
1. Our opening fern is explained: a fractal repeats one rule, so every part looks like the whole.
2. Nets turn solids into flat shapes, and a straight line on the right net is the shortest path on a box.
3. Front, top and side views, shadows and isometric drawings put solids on paper. Still open for you: draw one object at home in all three views and on isometric paper.
